books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, A. The Emergence of a National Culture

stimulus.text:
The table lists major works of the American Renaissance, the flowering of American literature in the early 1850s.

| Work | Author | Year |
|---|---|---|
| The Scarlet Letter | Nathaniel Hawthorne | 1850 |
| The House of the Seven Gables | Nathaniel Hawthorne | 1851 |
| Moby-Dick | Herman Melville | 1851 |
| Walden | Henry David Thoreau | 1854 |
| Leaves of Grass | Walt Whitman | 1855 |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 A, which names these five works as the peak of the American Renaissance in the early 1850s. Titles, authors, and years are as given in the book. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The works in the table are grouped together as the American Renaissance mainly because they did which of the following?

options.text: Were all written before 1800, in the colonial era
options.misconception: Old books feel like classics, so it is easy to push these famous titles a century earlier.

options.text: Were all plays performed in New York
options.misconception: New York was the publishing capital, so it is easy to turn these books into plays.

options.text: Were all written by Southern authors
options.misconception: The period's most famous region was the South, so it is easy to place these writers there.

options.text: American voices wrestling with religion, the past, and democracy

rationales.A: Every year in the table is 1850 or later; none of these books predates 1800.
rationales.B: These are novels, a book of essays in story form, and poems — none of them is a stage play.
rationales.C: Hawthorne, Melville, Thoreau, and Whitman were Northern writers, rooted in New England and New York.
rationales.D: A Puritan scarlet letter, a white whale, a pond cabin, and free verse all wrestle with America's past and promise.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the books share. Different authors, different forms, but all American subjects in American voices.
2. Ask what they wrestle with. Sin and the Puritan past, nature, democracy's promise and its contradictions.
Background from the books: this literature grappled with the Puritan legacy and the contradictions of the democratic experiment.
Remember: a literary movement is a shared set of questions, not a shared address.
